what: Every release of gen-z-developers.sgit.ai, narrated, oldest first. The newest row must be the version in admin/build/version.txt; build.py refuses otherwise.

releases.what: The first release, built from the newsroom's six gen-z-book articles and the two build briefs of 18 October 2026. v1.0.0 of the book (the 2018 first edition) imported verbatim from DinisCruz/Book_Generation_Z_Developer and shown chapter by chapter and on one page, outlines included; the versions page, reusing the newsroom's page_versions.py, with v1.0.0 frozen as markdown; the map, one row per 2018 file with the newsroom articles that answer it; the briefs captured; three roles (reviewer, editor, publisher) with their first issues and the editor's first interview script; the public working vault created and pushed with the working copy of v1, its read key published on the vault page; a private vault for the OpenRouter key, empty; the gate (validate.js) and the deploy pipeline, the same as the sibling sites.

The home page reviewed against the book's own assets and rebuilt around them: the 2018 cover in the hero with its eight lines (the newsroom article counted seven; Look under the hood was missed), and the first edition's public record on the page, the paperback on Amazon (139 pages, 30 September 2018, ISBN-10 1724194607, the two reader quotes) and the Leanpub edition (free to read online, 60% complete, 465 readers, 30,695 words), with the source on GitHub; the book card now dominates and the machinery sits smaller. The cover and the same references on the book's table of contents, the versions page and llms.txt. v1.0.0's date corrected to the paperback's publication, 30 September 2018; 8 October 2018 stays as the last change to the text.

The book as published, split from the drafts: the 2018 Hugo layouts put only chapters marked status: content in the Leanpub book and the print PDF, so the table of contents now shows those 28 chapters first, in the print edition's order with its page numbers (from the print-ready PDF Dinis supplied, now in the repository as v1/generation-z-print-ready.pdf, 139 pages), the GitHub-issues front-matter page included; the 6 drafts and 89 outlines follow, kept apart and marked. v1.0.0's frozen text is re-frozen as the published book (v0.1.0 had frozen the whole repository, drafts included); the drafts are kept beside it as v1/book/drafts.md and drafts.html, not part of any version. New: read/, the reader and the editor's desk: the book with its graph beside it (part, neighbours, chapters that share terms, the newsroom articles that answer it, the paragraphs as bars), chapter states (unread, reading, read, to review, continue, signed off), comments on paragraphs, filters and folds to focus, a reading meter after the newsroom's rules (a penny per 250 words read, £5 of credit, below zero allowed, nothing sent), and the export of the review as markdown for the vault's reviews/ folder or JSON; all kept in the browser. New: contributors/, who contributed to the first edition from the 2018 repository's git history and its GitHub issues and pull requests (20 people besides the author, 63 commits by others, 21 of 24 pull requests merged, 43 issues, 28 comments), with the data captured under admin/content/github/. The home page carries the split and the two new sections.

A journalist and its articles. The site gets its own articles section (/articles/, each article with a markdown twin to hand to an agent), written by a new role, the journalist (team/journalist/), in the newsroom's voice and shape, because an article is how Dinis briefs the roles that finish the book: the idea, the evidence and the task researched and counted on one page, ending with a brief a role can execute. Five articles: why briefs are written as articles, and the roles' names (reviewer, editor, publisher, journalist); releasing v1.0.0 again end to end, twice, first with the 2018 print file untouched and a new cover to prove the publishing half (cover, metadata, stamped files, a manifest, Leanpub, the paperback, a record of publications), then the same book built here with the graphs bookkit and checked against the 2018 file to prove the build half; one board for the book, with content issues pinned to a version and a quoted sentence, a Kanban page generated from the issue files, and the 43 GitHub issues of the 2018 repository (35 open) brought in; one inventory of everything unfinished (89 outlines, 23 draft-folder files, 6 unpublished chapters, the open issues, the handwritten notes); and the read, comment, decide loop on the editor's desk, with a short list of verbs and a decision file per item. A brief pointing at each article in the publisher's and the editor's briefs folders. No change to v1/ or to the book's version.

Dinis's first decisions, and a second stream of articles. Seven decisions from one voice memo, each a record on the new decisions page (/decisions/, sources in admin/content/decisions/) with his words: the 2018 text is CC BY 4.0; Leanpub gets our own PDF, built here with the graphs books' print workflow and matched page by page to the PDF Leanpub made in 2018, then the same for Amazon; every format (print, screen, EPUB, whatever Kindle needs) from one source; the cover waits; text issues and decisions on the text live in the vault, starting from v1.0.0 as site v0.2.0 froze it; every change is minor (the last number) unless Dinis says it is major, which is why this release is v0.2.2; and two kinds of article. The agent articles stream (admin/content/agent-articles/, /agent-articles/), in which each agent accounts for a significant body of work in its own voice, starts with the journalist's account of this work and these decisions. The co-written articles the decisions overturned are revised to say what is now true (the release plan, where content issues and text decisions live, the version numbers); the briefs are updated and the reviewer gets one (its licence issue can close); CLAUDE.md carries the version rule, the agent article rule and where decisions live; the footer, the home page and the versions page's licence note say CC BY 4.0.

The newsroom read in full for the book, and the book as storyboards drawn by code. The survey (admin/content/newsroom/survey.json, rendered at /map/newsroom.html): all 204 newsroom articles, the 107 sources and the 97 imported from sgit.ai, each classified bring (49), content (69), context (42) or skip (44) with its reason, 79 already cited by the map; 18 topics with the articles that feed them, 50 concepts with the article that defines each, and the gaps a newcomer needs that no article covers. The storyboards (/storyboards/): a cast of six characters who stand for the readers and the roles, and two storyboards of 15 panels each, the 2018 book and a first storyline for the second edition; each storyboard is JSON drawn in the browser by assets/storyboard.js with Rough.js 4.6.6 (MIT, vendored), sketched, animated in a swipe deck for an iPad, exportable to PNG with admin/build/storyboard_png.py; the build checks every panel against the cast and the renderer's vocabulary and, for the 2018 storyboard, every Guide line and quote card against the frozen text. A co-written article, start from the storyline, argues for starting the second edition there and briefs the editor; an agent article, storyboards drawn by code, accounts for the work. The cast, the storyline and the classes are proposals for Dinis.

The core idea of the second edition, in Dinis's words. A co-written article, you are lucky to be here: the book opens with wonder, not fear and not technologies (the first edition opened with a slide of logos and went too technical too soon); whoever reads it in 2026 or 2027 is lucky to be alive in this transition; nobody knows what happens next, and every transformation Dinis has lived through (the ZX Spectrum, the BBS, the internet, the mobile phone, the cloud, the apps, AI) came with the same warnings; this one is televised; technology can finally work for the reader after a generation of technology designed to hook them; learning can be made for each reader; craftspeople make their own tools, so the reader becomes a developer; think with the AI, it is still your name; and the opportunity includes the old jobs that never scaled. A storyboard of the opening in 16 panels, whose Guide lines and quote cards the build checks word for word against the article. A brief for the editor: record the decision in the vault, revise the first storyline's cold open, write the interview script, place the 2018 outlines this answers.

Wardley maps, and the reader's centre of gravity. A co-written article, where do you land?: maps run through the whole book and are shown before they are named; the four stages of evolution are not only for activities (Dinis's table from his Open Security Summit talk 'Why Wardley Maps changed how I think', Wardley's four rows and Dinis's ten more, transcribed); explorers, villagers and town planners described as personalities, each with a centre of gravity that can move over a career and its own skills and learning path; a black-and-white badge for each through the book. The storyboard renderer learns two things: a map panel kind that draws a Wardley map from data (anchor, value chain, evolution, movement arrows), with plain or named axes; and badges (compass, house, grid) shown by a character's name and on spectrum stops. The cast gets centres of gravity (Zara explorer, Priya villager, Tomás town planner, re-read from Dinis's descriptions), and storyboards 02 and 03 follow. A 14-panel storyboard, where do you land, quote-checked by the build against the article. A brief for the editor.

Paths and learning, in Dinis's words. A co-written article, connect the dots backwards: a path only makes sense looking back (Steve Jobs at Stanford, 12 June 2005, whose calligraphy class became the Mac's typography); the edge is now multidisciplinary, so the humanities and mathematics matter, though maths and music are taught as if to make people hate them (Paul Lockhart's A Mathematician's Lament; Dinis's memo had the first name wrong and the checking corrected it); generative AI lets the reader explore and communicate again, as the storyboards on this site show; learning is a lifelong skill that geography no longer decides, and the future is local and sovereign; reading this already puts the reader in a small minority; read it on paper, with a pen; and search gave answers where generative AI lets you ask for the evidence. A 14-panel storyboard, quote-checked by the build against the article, and a brief for the editor.

The influences, read for the book. A co-written article, where the thinking came from: Dinis's register at influences.sgit.ai, 25 people, works, communities and practices written as claims you can check, gone through entry by entry with where each lands in the book (Bret Victor and immediate connection in the opening; Csikszentmihalyi's flow and Ericsson's deliberate practice for the zone and learning; Wardley and Kevin Kelly for the frame; Popper and Schneier for questioning; Luhmann, Vannevar Bush and the semantic web for graphs and the future self; Torvalds, The Cathedral and the Bazaar, open source and OWASP for working and getting hired in the open; design, the design canon and Christopher Alexander for the villager's and town planner's craft; Sinek for why; David Rice, Neil Peart and playing in a band as interview material). It also records six things the 2018 book already wrote down that the register lists as unknown, and proposes a keep-your-own-register exercise for the reader. A 10-panel storyboard, quote-checked by the build; a brief for the editor; and the journalist's own blocked issue to brief the register, waiting on Dinis.

What the book means by generative AI. A co-written article, generative AI, not AI: AI is a huge bucket and the book is about the generative kind; Dinis's picture of how it works (a model builds its own representation and generates from it; a language model predicts the next word from a rich picture of how things connect, which is why a better prompt helps and why hallucinations happen; the image-extension tools of 2022 and 2023 that made it click; the patterns models found in our language; the wonder of what they can still turn out to do); and, because he asked to be corrected, a section of corrections with sources: classic machine learning learns too, the difference is predicting versus generating; inside a model there are vectors and attention, not a stored graph, so the graph is a metaphor; the prompt conditions rather than fine-tunes; next-token prediction plus training on feedback; a second cause of hallucinations from training that rewards guessing (Kalai and others, September 2025); diffusion for most image models; emergent abilities debated (Wei 2022, Schaeffer 2023). A note on the name (Gen Z, Gen AI, Gen Alpha born 2010 to 2024) left for the title interview. A 12-panel storyboard, quote-checked by the build, and a brief for the editor.

Questioning and evidence, and the David Rice keynote found. A co-written article, follow the rabbit holes: questioning and asking for the evidence is one of the most important skills now, and this generation already has much of it (good detectives, privacy-aware); provenance and explainability are how people can disagree rationally, including that not knowing can be a fact; following a rabbit hole is now a prompt away; managing information is what work is; generative AI makes what once cost hundreds of thousands of pounds a brief and a feedback loop, so be the best-prepared person in the room; and a proposed hands-on part for 2026, renewed yearly. A 10-panel storyboard, quote-checked by the build. The influences article now cites the recording Dinis shared, OWASP AppSec USA 2010: Keynote: David Rice, and the OWASP Summit 2011 working session on presenting his Pollution keynote; the journalist's register brief carries both. A brief for the editor.

The image that made generative AI click, found. Dinis shared the PDF of his keynote Deterministic GenAI Output With Provenance (v1.0, OWASP Global AppSec EU, Lisbon, 28 June 2024, 117 slides): slide 70, 'The image that caused my GenAI Paradigm Shift', is Lee Brimelow's post extending Van Gogh's The Starry Night with Photoshop's Generative Fill and Adobe Firefly. The article generative AI, not AI now names it, and adds slides 79 to 81 of the same talk: 'Input', 'Intermediate Representation', 'Output', the picture of generative AI Dinis described again in this week's memo, and human verification and ownership as what matters about the black box. Its storyboard panel and the editor's brief follow; the open question is now whether to ask Lee Brimelow for the image or remake the demonstration on the public-domain painting.

David Rice's keynote confirmed. Dinis's post The Pollution Analogy (11 December 2016) links the full recording of Upon the Threshold of Opportunity, the OWASP AppSec USA 2010 keynote, on Vimeo: the register's title and the YouTube recording are the same talk. The influences article now has the full recording, the post and its argument, quoted word for word (security risk as pollution: accepted, then regulated, then designed out; security does not need to say no all the time); the rabbit-holes article and its storyboard end the trail at the post; the journalist's brief for the register carries the anchor.

The book as a graph, and a librarian to keep it. A new admin area at /graph/, linked from the navigation, the home page and llms.txt: the ideas register (the core ideas read out of the co-written articles, the seven decisions, the newsroom survey's bring and content articles and the briefs, each with its statement, its provenance down to the section, the 2018 files it answers, a proposed chapter, a centre of gravity, and a state: accepted where Dinis said it in his own articles, otherwise a candidate for the loop); the sources page (every newsroom article, article, decision and 2018 file with what has been done with it, where a source becomes processed only when an idea cites it); a proposed chapter map (25 chapters in 9 parts, the first answer to the editor's blocked issue 003, with the hands-on part for 2026 that follow the rabbit holes proposes); the tasks page (every task the articles' briefs ask for, read from the articles by the build, with its state and the evidence in the repository); the plan, how an article becomes a chapter and the order of work from here; and the graph drawn, with graph.json for agents. The build refuses an idea that cites a source that does not exist, a chapter nothing names, or a source marked processed that nothing cites. The map gains the bring article the survey found missing (why my agents do not run on my laptop; the other three were already in). A librarian role (team/librarian/) with its first three issues, and a brief to the editor on the proposed map. Built on v0.2.11; the three articles released since v0.2.6 (the influences register; generative AI, not AI; follow the rabbit holes) are processed into the register too, and the image found in v0.2.10 moves task 4 of generative AI, not AI to blocked on Dinis's choice (ask for it, or remake it).

Graphs. A co-written article, everything is connected: a graph is a network of nodes and edges, not a diagram (as the graphs book Fractal Semantic Graphs defines it); the whodunit as the way in; a map is a graph with positions, and a Wardley map a graph with context; graphs of graphs, and nature as groups of groups forming abstraction layers; provenance as a graph; and start anywhere, because a graph has no front page. It shows the 2018 book was already there (the outline Graphs; the chapters Dot Language and AST) and lists what to bring from graphs.sgit.ai and the newsroom, chapters and figures. The storyboard renderer gains a graph panel kind: nodes and labelled edges with arrows, groups that nest, a highlighted path, and a detective style with a cork board, pinned notes and red string. A 12-panel storyboard uses all of it, quote-checked by the build. A brief for the editor. (Renumbered from v0.2.12 after another session released v0.2.10 to v0.2.12 in parallel.)

Article 14, Lenses, roles and loops, from Dinis's memo on how LLMs and agents work, co-written in his voice: a prompt is a lens (translating into another language and for a teenager, a musician, a doctor or a football fan are the same act to a model; 'bad at maths' is often the wrong lens); a role is a model with a description and a question; an agent is a role on a loop with a goal; tools are requests the model sends back, which the harness runs and resends with the next request, with the dates from ChatGPT to the Model Context Protocol; the model remembers nothing, hence the context window; long chats are compressed into lower-resolution summaries (the newsroom's eighteen summaries at 1.7%); so many focused, named threads, as in the email workflow. A 'Precisely' section makes the technical points exact (every request is independent, the model never runs a tool, memory features are still the context window). Storyboard 10, thirteen panels: five lenses on one idea, a role as a graph, the agent loop with one tool call, what the next request carries, the timeline, the compression bars, the named threads; every Guide line and quote card checked against the article by the build. The editor's brief.

The librarian's second pass: the bring class at zero, and the graphs chapter placed. The four newsroom bring articles the first pass left (no server by design; how the voice works; memory is not a spectator sport; code review as a fractal semantic graph) were read in full and processed into thirteen ideas: the file system as the database and no server by design (answering the 2018 outline Serverless from the other side), security as a business tool, open source as the reason it is easy to throw your own technology away; the voice as four inputs, the memo as the thinking, a correction that becomes a rule; memory as context management, the site as the memory, stale pages as false memories; code as a fractal semantic graph, reality as what corrects a graph, and the company in the review. The journalist's Everything is connected is processed into seven more (a graph is not a diagram, the whodunit board, a map as a graph with positions, graphs of graphs, provenance as a graph, start anywhere, the 2018 graph chapters), and the chapter map gains the graphs chapter it asks for, placed just before Where do you land with the order left as Dinis's question, plus Your first graph in the hands-on part. The journalist's Lenses, roles and loops, released meanwhile, is processed into five (a prompt is a lens, a role is a model with a description, tools changed everything, the model remembers nothing, long chats are compressed), with its chapter right after What generative AI is and two hands-on chapters (one idea five lenses; a tiny agent loop). 106 ideas; 30 chapters in 9 parts; the librarian's issue 001 closed with its answer and a debrief with the counts.

Two storyboard fixes Dinis asked for. The flick on moving forward: a panel used to arrive fully drawn and then blank and redraw itself when its play began; now a panel arrives as blank paper, plays once the first time it is reached, and stays drawn after that, going forward or back. Full screen on an iPad: Safari's prefixed full-screen styles were missing and the request can fail silently; the deck now uses the prefixed selectors, and where full screen is refused or absent it pins itself to the viewport with the same button (and Escape) to leave.

Storyboards you can process quickly, and faces that read the way they were meant to. Dinis asked for the animation to be optional, for a way to see the panels as a flow rather than one at a time, and said the Guide looked snarky and Tomás nearly always sad. The faces: the eyebrows were offset the same way on both eyes, so 'determined', 'worried' and 'thinking' drew one brow up and one down (a sardonic look) and 'happy' drew a frown under a smile; with the lopsided 'determined' mouth that was the snarky Guide, and 'thinking', Tomás's commonest mood, came out as a frown. Brows are now mirrored, the mouths are symmetric, and there are four new moods (excited, calm, sad, confused). The views: every storyboard opens as a deck, a grid (every panel on one page, one to six per row, each panel's text under it or beside it, a click plays a panel, Play in order plays them one after another) or a script (the storyboard as text: who is in each panel, their pose and mood, what they say, the evidence, the note and the source), with a filter and keys for everything. Animation is a setting, kept in the viewer's browser only; with it off a panel is simply there and Play shows its arrival on demand. New pages: every panel of every storyboard on one page (/storyboards/all.html), and the model sheet (/storyboards/model-sheet.html), every character in every mood and pose, to judge a drawing once rather than panel by panel. The night setting is now night. The build refuses an unknown setting or prop, which used to draw as nothing. storyboard_png.py no longer lets the site's sticky navigation cover the top of each panel, and --grid writes a whole storyboard as one contact-sheet image.

Article 15, The book in release mode, from Dinis's memo of 19 October 2026, co-written in his voice: run with the librarian's first list (the ideas register and the proposed chapter map) as the first release candidate of the book, rc1, in the vault; then rounds, each taking a pile (this site's articles, then the 2018 book, then the newsroom, and any new article) and ending in the next release candidate; and, from rc1 on, every idea, change and word goes through an adversarial review board, whose verdicts are kept with their reasons and become precedents, so it gets faster as it goes. Decision 008 records it. A new role, the review board (team/board/role.md): the advocate, the cutter, the readers (the cast), the checker and the editor, each in its own session, with Dinis deciding. Storyboard 11, fourteen panels, its Guide lines checked against the article by the build. Briefs to the editor (assemble rc1, the coherence read, clerk the board), the librarian (the batches, the verdicts, the convergence count), the reviewer (round 2, the 2018 book) and the publisher (what makes a release candidate official).

Gen Z Developers (GenAI Edition), release candidate 1: the first end-to-end draft of the second edition, built and readable. Dinis asked for a fully built first release candidate he could read, print and mark up, and named the book. 30 chapters in 9 parts, 50,607 words, written by seven agents in parallel from 109 of the register's 110 ideas under a style contract (Dinis's voice, no em-dashes, nothing not in a source) and a provenance rule: each chapter's front matter names its ideas, sources and 2018 files, and admin/build/book_v2.py refuses one that cites what does not exist. New at /v2/book/: the contents, one page per chapter with where it came from, the whole book on one page for print, a PDF, everything that waits on Dinis (34 notes), and the reader at /read/v2.html with its own store. The candidate is frozen once (v2/versions/v2.0.0-rc1.md, hash in admin/content/book/versions.json under candidates) and is not a version: decision 009 (a candidate is read on the site from a frozen snapshot; the working copy is the vault's book/rc1/) and decision 010 (the title). The release-mode article and decision 008 are processed into four ideas; the chapter map marks every chapter drafting with a link to its draft; the task parser knows the librarian and board roles. An agent article by the librarian says how it was done and what it leaves for each role.

Article 16, Gen ZX Developers, from Dinis's memo of 19 October 2026, co-written in his voice, as a proposal and the first change set from rc1 to rc2: the founder as the reader; the book for Generation Z and Generation X (the subject-matter experts starting companies, and often Generation Z's parents), with the millennials in the middle; Gen ZX as the plot twist back to the ZX Spectrum; explorer coding in place of vibe coding; one objective, that by the end of the book the reader has started a company, and the book measured by the companies created from it; Gen ZX Developers with the GenAI Startup Edition as the tagline, which would change decision 010's title. It maps what would change, part by part, against rc1 (a new part, Start the company; Building, safely becoming Build it without a server); lists the newsroom articles no idea cites yet that the startup edition would bring (pricing, funding without dilution, selling, sgit and privacy, RiskMandate, the cloud-credits table) and the gap articles the newsroom does not have (a UK limited company, Lithuania, Portugal, the EU, first customers, the community). The same memo decided three things: decision 011, precedents go on a list Dinis can overturn, and he reads the diffs of the book; decision 012, the book is 200 pages or more; decision 013, the hands-on part stays in the release candidate. Storyboard 12, fourteen panels; Marta, a Generation X expert founder and Zara's mother, proposed for the cast. Briefs to the editor (the change set for the board), the librarian (a variant chapter map, the startup articles), the publisher (what a new title means); the journalist's issue 002, the six gap articles.

Five themes across the whole site, and a top bar that fits. Dinis asked for the newsroom's five themes here, so the site reads in any of them, and for the menu to stop overflowing. The themes are newsroom.sgit.ai's, with the same values: Newsprint (the default, the look the site has had), Night, Paper, Blueprint and Ember, picked in the bar and remembered in the reader's browser only (localStorage genz.theme, nothing sent); with no choice made, a system set to dark gets Night. The theme is set before the first paint (assets/site.js, a classic script in the head), so a page never flashes Newsprint first. assets/themes.css holds every colour as a token, defined in all five themes, with this site's status colours (the badges, the graph's states, the reader's chapter states, the second edition's notes) as families of ink, line and fill; site.css, graph.css, reader.css, storyboard.css and print-book.css now read the tokens instead of some 190 literal colours, and the graphs drawn by script colour their nodes the same way. Kept as drawn in every theme, like printed pictures: the storyboard panels (cream paper), the book's navy cover band on the home page and the reader's navy bar, and code blocks (dark, as a terminal). Print is Newsprint whatever the theme, so the PDF build is unchanged. The bar: thirteen links on one row, which broke onto two or three lines below a wide screen, are now five groups (The book, Storyboards, Articles, The graph, The team), each a link with a menu under it, and the second edition sits in The book; the theme and the version sit together on the right, and below 1060px the groups fold behind a Menu button. The 'part of sgit.ai' pill moved to the footer.

Decision 014: Dinis named the second edition Generation ZX Developers (GenAI Startup Edition), replacing decision 010's Gen Z Developers (GenAI Edition), which stays on the record. The singular is deliberate, one name made of two generations and one letter from the 2018 title; the two generations are said on the cover line and in the opening; 'Gen ZX' is the short form, never 'XZ'; 'GenAI' is one word. rc1 is frozen and keeps the old title; rc2 carries the new one. Still Dinis's: second edition or a new book, and with it Leanpub, the ISBN, Amazon and the site's address. The Gen ZX article marks the title question answered; briefs to the publisher, the librarian and the editor.

The frame of release candidate 2, before its text. Dinis told the librarian to run with the Gen ZX proposal (decision 015, completing decision 014 on the title): the chapter map is rewritten for Generation ZX Developers (GenAI Startup Edition), 41 chapters in 10 parts, with a new first chapter, a new part Start the company at the centre, Building, safely rebuilt as Build it without a server, and four more hands-on chapters; the rc1 map is kept as chapters-rc1.json. The Gen ZX article and decisions 011 to 015 are processed into ideas (nine, the first of the rc2 batch); a candidate now carries its own title and chapter map, and while rc2 is being written the build renders rc1, the last finished candidate, and lists rc2 as in progress. New at /v2/book/: the rounds page (each round by size, the ideas that came in) and, once rc2 is frozen, the block-by-block diff Dinis reads (decision 011). The task parser knows the librarian and board roles. The rc2 text follows in the next release.

The gate learns about a candidate in progress. v0.2.23 shipped with the gate red: the versions page linked the frozen text of rc2, which is being written and has none yet, and the gate asked for its hash. A candidate marked in_progress now has no frozen text or hash to check, and the versions page says 'being written' for it instead of linking a file that does not exist. The release chain also stops on a red gate from now on rather than reading the last command's exit code.

The round-1 batch in the register. The newsroom articles Gen ZX Developers brought into scope for the startup edition (pricing, the miss-it test, selling shares rather than issuing them, the controllable founder, due diligence by agent, the company on code review, agentics ready to sell, eight months of SG/Send, the SaaS buyer's inertia, chat on a static site, the billing system, what sgit is and where the keys live, the value of constraints, ephemeral services, moving the cloud not the code, the startup credits table, RiskMandate's ten questions, the policy beside the prompt, the behaviour policy as business logic, open source is not free, who will fix your mess, the two lines on Lithuania, judo for small countries) were read in full by three readers and processed into 88 ideas marked batch rc2, with 37 existing ideas extended by a new source; the register now holds 198. Ten articles the survey had as context or skip are overridden to processed with a note that the proposal reclassified them. Every new idea is a candidate: Dinis brought the pile in, nobody has decided them. The rc2 chapters are being written from them.

Generation ZX Developers (GenAI Startup Edition), release candidate 2: the book rewritten under the Gen ZX frame, frozen and readable. 41 chapters in 10 parts, 73,314 words (+22,707 on rc1), written by seven agents from the rc1 chapters beside the 88 new ideas of the round-1 batch, under the same contract (Dinis's voice, nothing not in a source, keep what holds because Dinis reads the diff): a new first chapter, Gen ZX; the new part Start the company (be a founder, ship it and see if they miss it, price it then give it away, sell, fund it or do not, the company itself); Building, safely rebuilt as Build it without a server with a new Privacy by design chapter; Explorer coding, not vibe coding; four more hands-on chapters (form your company, the credits and programmes 2026, your first price and first ten customers, ship a serverless product in a weekend); the measure in the last chapter. Six chapters are honest placeholders that wait on Dinis's gap memos (the UK company, Lithuania, Portugal, the EU, the first customers, the community). 198 ideas written in, 47 notes for Dinis. New at /v2/book/: the rounds page counts the round by size and the diff page is the block-by-block diff from rc1 (decision 011); the PDF, the one-page view and the reader carry the new title. rc1 stays frozen at v2/versions/v2.0.0-rc1.md and in the vault's book/rc1/; rc2's working copy is the vault's book/rc2/. The librarian's round-1 debrief and the agent article's rc2 section say how it was done.

Synthetic readers, the frame, released before any reader runs. Dinis asked for five synthetic readers of release candidate 2, two from Generation Z, two from Generation X and one publisher who decides whether to commission it, to say on its pacing, content and structure what is strong and what does not make sense, and above all whether they would buy it. New at /readers/: the newsroom's synthetic-users method adapted from a website to a book (admin/content/readers/protocol.json: the text in place of the screenshot, a natural read that records where each reader puts the book down and whether they would buy it there, then an asked read as a beta reader, the same twelve interview questions for everyone and five more for the publisher, findings ordered by what they cost); the first study, 01-rc2, pinned to rc2's sha256, with the five invented readers (Aisha, Ellie, Nadia, Martin, Catherine) and what each was expected to do, written now so that the history shows the journeys came before the runs. The build refuses a run whose quotes are not word for word in the unit they cite. The editor's brief is team/editor/briefs/book__v2.0.0-rc2__synthetic-readers.md. The runs follow in the next release.
releases.why: A study is only honest if what was expected is on record before anything is run; and the pages had to exist for the runs to land on.

releases.what: Synthetic readers of release candidate 2: the five runs, the checks and the answer to Dinis's question, will they buy it. Nobody would buy rc2 as it stands; four of the five (Aisha and Ellie from Generation Z, Nadia from Generation X, and Catherine, the publisher, who would commission it with conditions) would once chapters 22 and 37, the company itself, are written; Martin, the sceptic, would not. Ratings 2, 3, 3, 3, 3. Three of the readers went from the contents page straight to Start the company or Hands on, and the sale was lost at the placeholders. Every finding that would change the book was checked against the frozen text: the hands-on part restates the chapters it follows (29% of chapter 13 is in chapter 30, 15% of 19 in 39), chapters 2 and 5 were marked too slow by all five, the book never mentions runway or leaving a salary, the worked examples are usually the author's own products, and Claude is named only in chapter 41. At /readers/01-rc2/: the answer, the five readers, expected against actual, twelve recommendations ordered by cost (six marked for Dinis), what is strong, the book unit by unit with each reader's mode, interest and pace, and a page per reader with the run, the interview and the findings; every finding with its check and a column for the editor's answer; the interviews question by question. The second edition's contents link to it. The agent article Five readers who do not exist tells how it was done.
releases.why: Dinis asked whether readers would buy the book and see its value, and how to make it better; the answer had to be checkable, so every quote is verified against the text and every finding that would change the book is checked before it is believed.

releases.what: An agent article by the journalist, Reading release candidate 2, and the first batch for the board, asked for by Dinis: rc2 acknowledged (41 chapters, 75,643 words, the Gen ZX frame, all 198 ideas of the register used, provenance on every chapter); a review from four parallel readings of every part and the frame chapter read in full, every repeated finding checked against the frozen text: what works (the promise, the chapters people would send on, testable rules, honesty, provenance, the voice) and ten improvements in order of cost (write the company; cut to length, not to a target; tell each story once; less of one estate and no product names in titles; the founder forward; the Generation Z route; four factual errors; date the money; the EU AI Act and other gaps; the making-of out of the reader's way). The first batch, drawn from the sources the register never cited (62 newsroom articles, 51 files of the 2018 book, six of them published chapters): five additions, each with its case, the cutter's objection and a recommendation (leaving a salary; every risk is already accepted; what your agents cost; one support agent, three designs; a company at the reader's scale), and five sign-offs, each setting a precedent (the 2018 tool and language chapters; the 2018 SRE chapter; the agent-governance commentary; the browser articles; the making-of). A brief to the editor to hear the ten.

The storyboards page as a comic shelf, the storyboards checked against the second release candidate, and a plan for panels in the book. Dinis asked for a far more visual storyboards page: the characters on it and a preview of every board. Three directions were drawn on a design canvas from real renders and he chose the comic shelf, now /storyboards/: the whole cast standing in a row in the hero, a board to start with (The opening) with play, grid and script, every storyboard as a comic cover with a strip of its next three panels, its number, the faces of the four characters seen most in it, its panel count and status, on three shelves, then the cast with their lines and more on demand, and how it works. Nothing on the page is an image file: build.py writes the text and an empty SVG per picture and storyboard.js draws them from the storyboards' own data, nearest the screen first and the rest while the browser is idle, so a corrected panel corrects its thumbnail. The shelves are data, admin/content/storyboards/shelves.json, and the build refuses a board on no shelf or on two. The gate's link check now ignores a query string, so a link to a storyboard's grid (?view=grid) is checked against its page. Asked whether the storyboards needed updating, the storyboards agent read all twelve against decisions 013 to 015 and rc2's map: board 12 now says the Gen ZX frame was adopted (decisions 014 and 015) rather than proposed, board 07's note on the name names decisions 010 and 014, board 08's hands-on panel names decision 013, every board's book version says the second edition exists as frozen release candidates, the cast file names both titles and records Marta as still a proposal, and board 02, the pre-Gen ZX storyline, is marked superseded. No Guide line or quote card changed. The agent article 'Storyboards on the shelf, and into the book' ranks six storyboards the second edition still needs (start the company first) and proposes, for Dinis to decide, five places for panels in the book (part openers, chapter strips, the cast as who the book is for, the hands-on storyboards chapter, how the book was made) and the pipeline that would print them: static SVG and PNG from the same build (decision 003), frozen with the candidate (decision 009), a black-and-white print mode, from rc3 since rc2 is frozen. Briefs for the librarian (the map's storyboard fields) and the publisher. Merges dev at v0.2.29.

Article 17, Version 2 on Leanpub, from Dinis's memo of 19 October 2026, co-written in his voice: Generation ZX Developers is a new book and version 2 of the 2018 one; Leanpub calls that an edition (a new book that past readers buy again), but the recommendation is to update the 2018 book in place as a new version, so its 465 readers get it free, the old address redirects (the book has had sales) and the 2018 text stays frozen here, on GitHub and in print. Pricing: the 2018 page today gives the book free only to Reader Members and asks everyone else for at least $7.99; the fix is two settings (free purchases allowed, the membership requirement off), with a minimum of $0, $20 suggested and $100 at most; Leanpub pays 80% from $7.99 up. The upload waits for a signed-off v2.0.0, unless Dinis decides to publish in progress. The listing ready to paste: title, subtitle, address, short description, about the book, the parts, categories, settings, and the release note to the 465. Every Leanpub rule sourced to its help centre as read that day. A brief to the publisher.

A new section, Infographics (/infographics/), and a new role, the illustrator, because Dinis asked for an infographics agent: what the book and the newsroom already have, what can be added, new infographics for the second edition, and a page to see the plan and review it. What exists: every one of the 2018 book's 31 images looked at, with a recommendation each (keep 2, redraw 6, replace 3, drop 13, keep 7 as the 2018 record; the only true infographics were someone else's, and three STEM figures were never generated); and the newsroom's 156 figures in the 46 articles the book draws on, catalogued from its graphs.json (the six gen-z-book articles have only eight). The plan: 81 proposals at four altitudes (the whole book, a part, a chapter, an area of the graph), every chapter of rc2 covered, 48 at priority 1, drafted by three reading agents a third of the book each, in the chapters' own words; 14 matched to a newsroom figure that already draws the idea. Ten drawn by a new renderer (admin/build/infographic_svg.py: a JSON spec in, a standalone SVG out, in the 2018 cover's palette, kept in every theme as a printed picture): the book on one page coloured by the synthetic readers, the three missing 2018 STEM figures, explorer/villager/town planner, the miss-it test, the card fee, sell don't issue, how cheap is it to undo, who can read what, reach/mandate/gap, and the one loop. The build refuses a quote or checked line not word for word in its chapter, an unknown chapter, source, idea, form or state, a decided proposal without the name of who decided, and a 2018 image with no row. The plan page has a review in the browser (accept, change, decline, later, with a note; exported as markdown or JSON for the vault; nothing sent). Written up in the agent article Infographics at every altitude, which also says how this plan shares the book's pages with the storyboards agent's. Nothing is decided: every proposal waits on Dinis.

Covers (/covers/): three cover designs for Generation ZX Developers (GenAI Startup Edition), because Dinis asked for covers that can go to Amazon, made in SVG so they can be resized and changed, with a system behind them; decision 004 had held the cover until he asked. A generator (admin/build/covers.py) draws each design as a function of width and height, so one layout makes the 6 by 9 inch front (and Leanpub's 1,800 by 2,700 JPEG), the Kindle cover at 1,600 by 2,560 (laid out again for its taller shape) and the KDP paperback's full wrap with 0.125 inch bleed and a spine computed from the page count (12.745 by 9.25 inches for an assumed 220 pages), as a print-ready PDF with its fonts embedded and its page exactly that size. The SVG is the master, with live text and open-licensed fonts embedded (fetched with their licences by cover_fonts.py). The designs: ZX, the book as a graph (drawn from the candidate's own chapters and ideas), and One letter more (the 2018 cover with an X added). An art-director agent reviewed the first renders and ranked ZX first and the graph second; its fixes are applied, and two of its rules are now gates: every word of the title must read at Amazon's thumbnail on every front, and nothing on the back may reach the barcode area. The build checks every word on the covers against its source (decision 014, article 17, the first edition's cover). Written up in the agent article Three covers drawn by code. Proposals: nothing is chosen until Dinis chooses.
